newsitem.title: MOZAMBIQUE: Mozambique to host anti-landmine conference.
newsitem.headline: Mozambique to host anti-landmine conference.

text.p: With the support of Graca Machel, widow of Mozambique's first president, Africa will take the lead in February in the battle to ban one of the most brutal weapons of war.

More than 300 activists from around the world are due to meet in Mozambique's capital, Maputo, to step up the international campaign against landmines, conference organiser Julio Mapote told Reuters on Tuesday.

Mozambique, embroiled in vicious wars from the mid-60s to the early 90s, is strewn with unexploded landmines. On average, unlucky Mozambicans and wandering children detonate 40 of them per month. Amputees are a common sight in Maputo.
The conference, between February 25 and 28, has the backing of Graca Machel one of Africa's most prestigious figures.
Graca, 51, who joined the Frelimo independence guerrilla movement in 1973, recently presented a highly-praised United Nations report on the impact of armed conflict on children.
Her husband, Samora Machel, the Frelimo military commander, became president at 1975 independence. He was killed in a plane crash in South Africa in 1986.

Graca's Foundation for Community Development is one of the member organisations of the Mozambican Campaign against Landmines, a group which is pressuring the Mozambican government to subscribe to an international ban on mines.
"Graca gave us space in her foundation's offices and she supports our cause," said Mapote.
Mozambique was at war between 1964 and 1992, first with the Portuguese colonial regime, then with Ian Smith's Rhodesia, then with South-African backed rebels.
All sides used land mines, a cheap and deadly weapon that many countries say they must retain in their arsenals.

Nobody knows how many mines still lie scattered across the Mozambican countryside, but the international group Human Rights Watch estimates that "the number is certainly in the tens if not hundreds of thousands".
Since 1993 the United Nations has been responsible for a national mine clearance programme.
There are an estimated 10,000 amputees in Mozambique who have received some form of medical treatment. One-legged beggars on crutches are a common sight in cities.
"An average of 40 Mozambicans detonate landmines every month. Eighty per cent of them are children," said Mapote.

"We have received notification from about 100 southern African organisations, about 100 from other African countries and about 100 from other continents, saying they will attend the conference," Mapote said.
